notes:
Task and constraints: Count words that can be stretched to match S by expanding runs of repeated characters.
Idea: Run-length encode S and each candidate, then compare run characters and counts.
Technique and why it applies: Matching run-character sequences are necessary. Each candidate run must either match the target run length or be stretchable because the target run has length at least three and is no shorter than the candidate.
Invariant: R and count describe the target's run symbols and lengths; R2 and count2 describe a candidate.
Edge cases: The code unpacks zip(*[]) for an empty S or word, which raises an error. Standard constraints generally provide nonempty strings.
Complexity: Run-length encoding and comparisons take O(total characters) time and O(n) temporary space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether the first player wins the chalkboard XOR game under optimal play.
Idea: Apply the known XOR-game characterization: the first player wins if the total XOR is zero or the number of elements is even.
Technique and why it applies: If XOR is zero, the first player wins immediately. Otherwise, an even number of elements lets the first player maintain a winning parity argument under optimal play.
Invariant: The expression computes the XOR of all values and checks the parity of nums length.
Edge cases: functools and operator are referenced without imports in the snippet, so it fails unless those names are defined externally. reduce also requires a nonempty sequence, though the problem supplies at least one value.
Complexity: XOR reduction takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Check whether the first player wins the chalkboard XOR game.
Idea: Compute the XOR of all elements and apply the even-length winning condition.
Technique and why it applies: A zero XOR gives an immediate win; otherwise, an even count guarantees a winning strategy for the first player.
Invariant: reduce(xor, nums) is the XOR of the full array.
Edge cases: The imports are present, but reduce(xor, nums) would fail on an empty list; the standard constraints make nums nonempty.
Complexity: The reduction takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

Task and constraints: Aggregate visit counts for each domain and all of its parent subdomains.
Idea: Split each count-domain entry into labels and accumulate the count for each suffix domain.
Technique and why it applies: Rebuilding suffixes from the right creates entries such as example.com and com, so every visit contributes to the full domain and each parent.
Invariant: output maps each subdomain string to its total visit count.
Edge cases: The code prints intermediate lists and subdomains, causing debug output. Counts are parsed as integers; domains without dots still produce one suffix.
Complexity: For total input domain characters T, suffix construction is O(T²) in the worst case due to repeated string concatenation, and storage is O(number of distinct subdomains).

Task and constraints: Return visit totals for each domain and every parent subdomain.
Idea: Split each domain into labels and accumulate counts while joining suffixes from right to left.
Technique and why it applies: Each iteration extends curr by one label and updates the corresponding suffix total, including the top-level domain.
Invariant: result maps each encountered suffix to the sum of all visits that include it.
Edge cases: split() handles extra whitespace more robustly than splitting on one literal space. Output order follows dictionary insertion order and is not required to be sorted.
Complexity: Joining suffix labels repeatedly costs O(T²) in the worst case for long domains; storage is O(D) for D distinct suffixes.

Task and constraints: Find the largest area formed by any three points in the plane.
Idea: Enumerate every three-point combination and compute its triangle area with the determinant formula.
Technique and why it applies: The absolute cross-product expression gives twice the triangle area; multiplying by one half yields the area regardless of point orientation.
Invariant: maxA stores the largest area found among all triples processed so far.
Edge cases: Collinear triples produce zero area. Fewer than three points yield zero because no combinations are generated.
Complexity: There are O(n³) triples, each evaluated in constant time, giving O(n³) time and O(1) auxiliary space apart from the combinations iterator.

Task and constraints: Return the largest triangle area possible from the given points.
Idea: Check all index triples and keep the maximum shoelace/determinant area.
Technique and why it applies: The determinant formula computes the area of each triangle using its three coordinates; the absolute value handles either orientation.
Invariant: result is the maximum area among all triples visited so far.
Edge cases: Repeated or collinear points can yield zero area and do not break the calculation. Fewer than three points leave result at zero.
Complexity: Three nested loops enumerate O(n³) triples with O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Partition array A into at most k nonempty groups to maximize the sum of group averages.
Idea: Use one-dimensional dynamic programming, starting from suffix averages and refining the best value as the number of cuts increases.
Technique and why it applies: For each cut count l and start i, the code considers a first segment ending at j and combines its average with dp[j+1], which represents the remaining suffix.
Invariant: dp[i] is the best average sum for suffix A[i:] using the number of groups represented by the current outer iteration.
Edge cases: The variable name sum shadows Python's built-in. The loops assume k<=n; invalid larger k can make the intended partition count unclear.
Complexity: The nested cut, start, and endpoint loops take O(kn²) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of buses needed to travel from source to target using fixed bus routes.
Idea: Build a stop-to-route graph and breadth-first search over reachable stops, incrementing the count when boarding a bus.
Technique and why it applies: Each visited stop exposes routes serving it; each bus is processed once, and its stops are enqueued with count+1.
Invariant: bfs stores a stop and the number of buses used to reach it; seen_buses prevents processing the same route repeatedly.
Edge cases: defaultdict and deque are imported as class attributes, which Python resolves in method scope through the class namespace in this code. If source equals target, zero buses are needed.
Complexity: Each route is explored at most once and its stops are scanned once, giving O(total route stops) time and space.

Task and constraints: Return the fewest buses needed to travel from S to T.
Idea: Explore reachable stops in BFS layers, where each layer corresponds to one additional bus.
Technique and why it applies: The stop-to-route mapping finds buses boarding at each stop. A route's stops are discovered and added to the next layer; lookup prevents revisiting stops.
Invariant: q contains stops reachable using result buses, and result is incremented after each layer.
Edge cases: S==T returns zero. The code removes a route from to_route[next_stop] while iterating a different stop's route set; this can mutate a set being iterated only if it is the same set object, which is not generally the case, but it is a fragile optimization.
Complexity: Route stops are processed with sets and queues; expected time and space are O(total route stops).

Task and constraints: Generate all valid coordinate pairs by inserting a decimal point into each side of the digit string.
Idea: Split the digits into left and right coordinate parts, then enumerate legal decimal placements for each part.
Technique and why it applies: _splitToNums rejects integer parts with leading zeros and fractional parts with trailing zeros. Cartesian products combine valid x and y forms.
Invariant: Each emitted coordinate pair uses the original digit order and has valid decimal formatting on both sides.
Edge cases: re and itertools are not imported in the snippet. The regex string includes slashes as literal characters, so it does not behave like a slash-delimited regex and may fail to reject all-zero parts as intended.
Complexity: The number of splits and decimal placements can produce O(n^4) candidates in a loose bound, with output-dependent space.

Task and constraints: Return all valid coordinate representations from a parenthesized digit string.
Idea: Enumerate split points and generate legal integer/decimal forms for each side.
Technique and why it applies: A left part may not have leading zeros unless it is exactly zero; a nonempty fractional part may not end in zero. itertools.product combines every valid left and right representation.
Invariant: make yields only legal numeric forms for the requested substring, and the comprehension pairs forms from both sides.
Edge cases: The outer loops exclude the parentheses and consider each nonempty split. If the right part is empty, make can emit an integer, though the chosen split bounds normally keep both parts nonempty.
Complexity: Candidate generation is polynomial in digit length, with output-sensitive space for all returned coordinate strings.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of instructions to drive a race car from position 0 to target.
Idea: Run breadth-first search over states consisting of position and speed.
Technique and why it applies: Accelerate doubles speed and advances position; reverse keeps position fixed and resets speed to ±1. BFS layers represent instruction counts, so the first target state gives the minimum.
Invariant: Each queued pair is reachable using the current number of instructions, tracked by steps.
Edge cases: q.pop(0) is linear-time for a Python list, making queue operations expensive. The reverse condition's boolean precedence should be reviewed; there is no visited set or explicit bound, so the search can revisit states and grow without bound.
Complexity: This unbounded BFS can explore many repeated states; with a proper bounded state space it would be O(number of states), but this implementation has no finite complexity guarantee.

Task and constraints: Compute the minimum instruction count for a race car to reach target.
Idea: Build a DP over target positions, considering exact acceleration runs and sequences that overshoot then reverse.
Technique and why it applies: If i equals 2^k-1, k accelerations reach it exactly. Otherwise, the code compares overshooting and reversing with shorter accelerate-reverse-accelerate-reverse constructions.
Invariant: dp[i] is the minimum instruction count to reach position i from zero with speed one.
Edge cases: The recurrence only references smaller positions, so previously computed DP entries are available. target=0 returns dp[0]=0.
Complexity: Each i performs O(log i) candidate checks, yielding O(target log target) time and O(target) space.

Task and constraints: Find the most frequent word in a paragraph that is not in banned.
Idea: Normalize punctuation and case, count word occurrences, remove banned words, then return the most common remaining word.
Technique and why it applies: Counter provides word frequencies, and deleting banned keys ensures the most-common query considers only allowed words.
Invariant: para_count holds frequencies for normalized words not yet removed as banned.
Edge cases: string and Counter are class-level imports referenced from the method; lookup depends on Python class-scope resolution and may be fragile. If every word is banned or the paragraph is empty, most_common(1)[0] raises an error.
Complexity: Normalization and counting are O(P) expected time for paragraph length P, with O(U) space for distinct words.

Task and constraints: Return the most frequent non-banned word in a paragraph.
Idea: Lowercase and split the paragraph, count words, and select the highest-frequency word not in the banned set.
Technique and why it applies: Counter stores frequencies; the scan updates result only when a non-banned word has a strictly greater count, preserving the first encountered tie.
Invariant: result is the best eligible word encountered so far, or empty if none has been selected.
Edge cases: strip removes only the listed punctuation characters at word boundaries, not punctuation embedded inside a token or all punctuation from the paragraph. If no eligible word remains, the function returns an empty string.
Complexity: Counting and scanning take O(P) expected time and O(U) space for U distinct tokens.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest reference string encoding all words as suffixes followed by a # delimiter.
Idea: Insert reversed unique words into a trie and count the lengths of words whose terminal nodes are leaves.
Technique and why it applies: A word that is a suffix of another word ends at an internal trie node and needs no separate encoding. Leaf words contribute len(word)+1 characters.
Invariant: trie_root represents reversed prefixes, and tail_nodes pairs each unique word's terminal node with its encoded length.
Edge cases: Duplicate words are removed first. Empty words produce a terminal root node and contribute one delimiter character under this implementation.
Complexity: Trie construction takes O(total characters) expected time and space.

Task and constraints: Compute the minimum length of a reference string that encodes each word as a suffix.
Idea: Build a trie of reversed unique words and count only words whose terminal trie node has no children.
Technique and why it applies: If one reversed word is a prefix of another, the shorter original word is a suffix and can share the longer encoding. Leaf terminal nodes identify words requiring their own ending marker.
Invariant: nodes[i] is the trie node reached by traversing the reversed form of words[i].
Edge cases: Duplicate words are removed before building the trie. reduce is imported but unused; functools.reduce is used to traverse dictionary keys.
Complexity: Trie construction and terminal checks take O(total characters) expected time and O(total trie nodes) space.

Task and constraints: For each character in s, return its distance to the nearest occurrence of c.
Idea: Collect every index of c and check every string position against all such indices.
Technique and why it applies: The minimum absolute index difference is the shortest distance to any occurrence.
Invariant: ch contains all positions where s equals c, and each appended result is the minimum distance for that position.
Edge cases: If c does not appear, the code returns len(s) for every position, which is not a valid nearest distance but such input is excluded by the problem. Empty s returns an empty list.
Complexity: With n characters and m occurrences of c, time is O(nm) and space is O(n+m).

Task and constraints: Compute the distance from every position in S to the nearest occurrence of C.
Idea: Make a forward and backward pass, carrying the most recently seen occurrence in each direction.
Technique and why it applies: The forward pass captures nearest occurrences to the left; the reverse pass improves each answer using the nearest occurrence to the right.
Invariant: prev is the latest C index encountered in the current scan direction, and result[i] is the best distance found so far.
Edge cases: If C is absent, all answers remain len(S), although the problem guarantees at least one occurrence. The initial negative prev makes the forward pass's distance large until C appears.
Complexity: Two scans take O(n) time and O(n) result space.
